analysis.one_liner: Gives wheelchair owners and independent shops the legal right and tools to repair power wheelchairs.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in August 2025 with one cosponsor and referred to two House committees, where it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it legal to bypass the electronic locks on powered wheelchairs and other mobility devices so owners and independent repair shops can diagnose, maintain, and fix them. It would require the manufacturers to sell repair parts, manuals, software, and diagnostic tools to independent shops and device owners on the same terms they give their own authorized dealers. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would enforce these requirements.
analysis.who_benefits: People who use power wheelchairs, scooters, and wearable robotic walking devices, along with the independent repair shops that fix them. Today, a wheelchair owner who needs a repair may have to wait weeks for the manufacturer's authorized service network, and copyright law can make it illegal for anyone else to bypass the device's software locks. The bill would let owners and independent shops do repairs themselves and buy the needed parts and tools at the same price and terms the manufacturer offers its authorized dealers, which could mean faster fixes, lower repair bills, and less time stuck without a working chair [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Power wheelchair users and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: It adds a copyright-law exception making it legal to circumvent software locks for the purpose of diagnosing, maintaining, or repairing a powered mobility device, and to make or distribute the tools needed to do so [S2].

It requires manufacturers to provide documentation, parts, embedded software, firmware, and repair tools to independent repair providers and owners on a timely basis and on terms equivalent to the best terms offered to their own authorized repair network, including tools to disable and reset electronic security locks [S2].

It gives the Federal Trade Commission enforcement authority and lets state attorneys general sue in court to stop violations and obtain civil penalties, damages, and restitution for state residents [S2].
It requires manufacturers to notify buyers and independent shops of these repair rights and to set up a standard public process for requesting repair materials within 90 days of enactment [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of powered wheelchairs and other mobility devices, which would have to sell repair parts, manuals, diagnostic software, and unlocking tools to independent shops and owners on equal terms, ending their control over who can service their devices and over repair pricing. Some repair revenue now captured through authorized dealer networks would shift to independent shops and owners [S2].

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers would have to provide tools to disable electronic security locks and reset them after repair, which raises safety and cybersecurity concerns about who can alter the software controlling a device a disabled person depends on; the bill addresses this only by allowing delivery through a secure data release system [S2].

The bill protects manufacturers and authorized dealers from liability for damage or injury caused by an independent shop's or owner's repair, so a botched third-party repair would leave the device owner with limited recourse against the manufacturer [S2].

It does not require manufacturers to sell parts that are no longer available, and it preserves trade secrets except as needed to supply required repair materials, so owners of older devices may still be unable to get parts [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people who use these devices, the benefits are concrete: a broken power wheelchair can leave someone housebound, and manufacturer-controlled service often means long waits and high repair prices. The main costs fall on manufacturers, who lose a repair monopoly. The real drawbacks are design questions: loosening software locks on safety-critical devices needs careful handling, and the liability shield for manufacturers shifts risk onto owners who use independent repairs. On balance the bill targets a narrow, well-documented hardship for a vulnerable population, with manageable if real trade-offs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill is sitting with two House committees after referral and no hearings, votes, or further action have been scheduled.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 26, 2025 by Rep. Maxwell Frost with Rep. Perez as the sole cosponsor [S1].

It was referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Judiciary Committee, the standard first step that sends a bill to the panels with authority over its subject matter [S4].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — has been taken since referral, and the 119th Congress is still in session [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, powered mobility device manufacturers are better off: the status quo, in which they control who can repair their devices and what repairs cost, remains unchanged while the bill sits in committee.

for.name: Rep. Maxwell Frost
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Wheelchair Right to Repair Act in the House.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a Democratic sponsor and its single cosponsor is also a Democrat, so no partisan pattern has yet emerged; no member has opposed it on the record.

industries.industry: Powered wheelchair and mobility device manufacturers
industries.note: The bill ends these manufacturers' control over who can service their devices by requiring them to sell parts, manuals, software, and unlocking tools to independent shops and owners on the same terms offered to their authorized dealers. Repair is a lucrative add-on to device sales, and owners of these devices have limited alternatives when manufacturer service is slow or expensive.

industries.industry: Independent repair shops for mobility equipment
industries.note: Independent shops gain legal access to parts, diagnostic software, and documentation they are often locked out of today, letting them compete for repair work. Their interest in the bill runs with that of device owners, who get faster and likely cheaper repairs.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is at the very start of the process with a single cosponsor and dual committee referral, which splits jurisdiction and makes advance harder. Most House bills never get a hearing or a vote, and with no committee action more than a year before the Congress ends, the realistic outlook is that it stalls in committee unless it picks up substantially more cosponsors and advocacy pressure.
